blocks.text: So when we read in the Sacred text that in the famine of Samaria a quarter of a cab of dove's dung sold for five pieces of silver, why should we not understand the chickpea, or a kind of chickpea? Certainly everything will then fit nicely. 1. First, that the chickpea was very well known in Judaea is shown, besides several places of the Talmud, by the Sacred History in the passage cited above from 2 Sam. XVII, 28., where the Gileadites and Ammonites bring David, among other things, קלי kali, that is, roasted chickpea. Accordingly חמצה, that is, Emesa, [col. 48] a famous city on the border of Judaea, which had its own kings, seems to have been named from the chickpea. Belon, in book 2, chapter 53 of his Singularia, observes that in the Egyptian city of Cairo there are many shops in which nothing is sold but roasted chickpea, which is bought in great quantity by the pilgrims who set out from there every year for Mecca. And in chapter 99 he reports the same of Damascus: In Damascus, he says, there are many shops in which all are occupied with roasting chickpeas. They call them Erevithia (ἐρεβίνθια [erebinthia]) by a Greek name. Roasted and dried in bronze pans, they are very convenient for those who undertake a long journey. 2. Further, the cab is a measure of legumes as well as of grain. For legumes, just like grain, have their seeds, which the Arabs designate by the common name حبوب [ḥubūb]. 3. That some cheap kind of food is signified by dove's dung is clear from these words of the Sacred text: An ass's head was sold for eighty shekels, and a quarter of a cab of dove's dung for five shekels. For there dove's dung is compared with the ass's head: the latter was for sale at eighty shekels, a quarter of a cab of the former at five shekels. So a whole cab, which is the measure of a day's food, cost twenty shekels, and four cabs eighty shekels, the price at which an ass's head was then sold. Therefore, whatever you understand there by dove's dung, it must plainly have been a very cheap food, since four cabs of it, that is, as much as suffices a sober man for four days' sustenance, were valued no higher than one ass's head. Now among foods in common use hardly anything is cheaper than the chickpea. Accordingly the chickpea is the food only of [II, 586] the frugal or the poorer sort. Thus in Aristophanes' Peace, as noted above, a certain countryman wishes to be with his companions,
Ἀνθρακίζων τοὐρεβίνθου, Τήν τε φηγὸν ἐμπυρεύων· [Anthrakizōn tourebinthou, Tēn te phēgon empyreuōn]

Toasting the chickpea over the coals, and roasting the beech-nut at the fire. In Alexis the Comic poet, in Athenaeus book 2, an old woman lamenting her poverty lists, among the common foods by which she barely sustains her wretched life, ἐρέβινθον [erebinthon] and λάθυρον [lathyron], that is, chickpea and chickling. Horace, book 1, Satire 6, to show that he is content with little and that a meagre diet suffices him:
— — — thence I take myself home to a dish of leeks and chickpeas and fritters.
And in the De Arte he thus contrasts the rich with those who live on roasted chickpeas and nuts:
For those who have a horse, a father and property take offence, nor, if the buyer of roasted chickpeas and nuts approves something, do they receive it with fair minds or bestow a crown.
Hence that line of Martial, book 5, Epigram 79:
Both hot chickpea and warm lupin, it is a small little dinner, who can deny it?
And book 1, Epigram 104, on the miser Scaevola, who cheated his own appetite:
And the thick dregs of reddish Veientan are drunk: warm chickpea costs an as, and an as buys Venus.
And Epigram 42 of the same book:
— — — — — — he who sells soaked chickpea to the idle crowd. — —

That is, he who peddles the cheapest foods, among them soaked chickpea, to the common people on holiday, at leisure for the Circus and the stage. To the same effect is the fact that at Rome, at the shows, those canvassing for office, to win the favour of the populace, scattered chickpeas along with beans and lupins among the gifts thrown to the crowd. To this allude these words of Horace, book 2, Satire 3:
May you squander your goods on chickpeas, beans and lupins, so that you may strut broad in the Circus and stand in bronze.
